newsitem.title: HUNGARY: EU official's warning on expansion worries Hungary.
newsitem.headline: EU official's warning on expansion worries Hungary.

text.p: The European Union's representative in Hungary surprised the Hungarian government on Friday by publicly saying the idea that central European states could join the EU before 2002 was "an illusion".

"It would be an illusion for anyone to think the membership is possible before January 1, 2002," Hans Beck, head of the EU's mission in Budapest told a conference on Hungary's media privatisation in Budapest.

"The negotiations will probably start at the beginning of 1998," Beck told Reuters. "Let's say you have the negotiations for two years, then you have the ratification process in the member states. In view of our previous experience of expansion it is too optimistic to say even 2001."

Hungary's government expressed alarm at Beck's statement. "I do not agree with him in that respect," Istvan Szent-Ivanyi, state secretary at Hungary's foreign ministry, told Reuters. "I am firmly confident the pre-planned timetable can be kept."

Countries of the former Warsaw Pact and the Mediterranean who have formally applied to join the EU have been told that full negotiations will begin six months after the current Inter-Governmental Conference (IGC) ends.

The IGC is working out institutional reform within the Union which would allow further expansion and has been given a target of June 1997 to complete its work. Should the target be met, the EU Commission has talked of full membership for the first successful applicants by 2002 at the latest.

"We are of course expecting a period of mutual adjustment for two, three or five years but at least legal membership should start before," Szent-Ivanyi said. "We are looking at 2000 as the year of membership."
Later, Beck played down the difference in dates. "I agree when my Hungarian colleagues when they say around the year 2000 but I think 2002 is still around the year 2000," he said.

At an EU summit in Dublin ealier this month, EU leaders pledged to press on with negotiations to prepare their bloc for an influx of new members from central and eastern Europe and the Mediterranean by the start of the new century.
But the summit was dominated by fears among leaders that their plans for reforming the bloc to accept new countries from eastern Europe and the Mediterranean were on shaky ground.
